v1.feedback: The Physarum-to-amulet concept is legible but the execution is shallow — the parent's slime-mold network is demoted to a 2D texture on a flattened sphere, so the 'talisman' transformation reads as 'put the old thing on a medallion' rather than a deep morphological change. Lift the trail field into 3D: extrude high-intensity trails as raised inscription geometry (displacement map or instanced tube curves along trail ridges) so the disc has actual sculptural relief, not just a painted-on pattern. The gemstone nodes are tiny additive spheres that don't interact with the disc surface — embed them as concavities or faceted insets that catch the rim light. Finally, the gentle spin is safe but static; consider a slow breathing scale-pulse on the disc thickness keyed to total trail energy so the object feels alive rather than decorative.

v2.feedback: The physarum-to-relief-carving concept is a genuine morph of the parent's slime-mold substrate into a talisman object — the idea clearly drove the design rather than being a cosmetic rename. The disc fills the frame well and the oxidized bronze/jade palette is restrained and earned. Two issues: the flat disc reads more as a textured plane than a carved amulet — beveling the disc edge or adding a slight convex dome would sell the 'stone object' read in under 2 seconds; and the rim light calculation in the fragment shader uses a fixed vec3(0,0,1) eye direction rather than the actual view vector, which kills the rim-light payoff during the slow orbit rotation. Fix the rim to use normalize(cameraPosition - vPos) and add a subtle chamfer geometry at the disc boundary to land the talisman silhouette.
